newsitem.title: USA: OPTIONS - U.S. debt volatilities steady, off highs.
newsitem.headline: OPTIONS - U.S. debt volatilities steady, off highs.

text.p: Implied volatilities for U.S. fixed income options were little changed after slipping from early highs in choppy trading ahead of the March 25 Federal Open Market Committee meeting, dealers said.

Volatilities were bid when underlying markets tumbled early in the day on a slightly higher than expected February consumer price index. But the bids soon dissipated as underlying prices held above key support levels.
"Basically, it's been pretty steady," a brokerage trader at the Chicago Board of Trade said of Treasury bond volatilities. "Everyone's just waiting for FOMC."

Implied volatilities for CBOT May and June T-bond options stood at around 9.6 and 9.5 percent respectively shortly before the close, up marginaly from late Tuesday levels but off some 0.2 point from early highs.

February CPI was up 0.3 percent overall in February against an average Wall Street estimate of a 0.2 percent rise and January's 0.1 percent gain. The core CPI, excluding food and energy, was up 0.2 percent, in line with expectations.
Among the few large option deals today, an investment bank that was a big buyer of puts in recent weeks was seen buying 4,000 legs of May 106/108 put spreads.
April options which expire at the end of the week saw mixed flows in moderate sizes.
Traders said Federal Reserve chairman Alan Greenspan's testimony before a House banking and financial services subcommittee offered no market-moving remarks.
But they added that the market would keep an eye on Greenspan when he speaks again on Thursday before the Joint Economic Committee.
At the shorter end of the yield curve, Eurodollar volatilities were steady to firmer on lingering Fed tightening concerns.
Implied volatility for September Eurodollar futures options was up 0.1 point at around 12.8 percent, while December was steady at around 14.1 percent.
"The way the (futures) market rejected the attempt to rally back up after the number this morning was pretty negative," said an investment bank at the Chicago Mercantile Exchange.
"We haven't exactly taken out key levels -- we sort of held the lows from the unemployment break (93.840 in September futures on March 7)," he noted. "But I just think it's a matter of time."
September futures dipped to a low of 93.850 early in the session.

The investment bank trader said even June futures, which were seen to have priced-in a 25 basis point rate hike, were still vulnerable because the Fed could raise rates by 50 basis points perhaps in May if it did not tighten at the March FOMC meeting.

Among the larger deals, an investment bank was seen selling June 94.25 calls and bought 94.00 puts in a 6,000-lot combo trade, while a European firm sold December 94.00 calls and bought 94.25 calls in a 3,000-by-6,000 ratio spread.
